The game is good, but optimization suffers greatly - despite being low-poly game without seemingly very detailed textures and shaders, on some stages even GTX 2080 is unable to hit 60 FPS in windowed game covering roughly 1/2 of full HD screen, meaning you can't do anything demanding or play other games while having The Perfect Tower II in background, despite it being idle game. I can recommend this game after it will be optimized, but it's hard to recommend it in current state.

以前很爱玩的Flash游戏，续作登录steam了 塔防部分变成了关卡制，各种系统也变得更丰富了，但是没中文只能边猜边玩比较痛苦 POWER PLANT：发电站，在“POWERGRID”中建造设施产生电力，在“NETWORK”中消耗电力提升其他建筑物效率 MINE：矿场，左侧面板可以升级钻头功率/油箱容量/油耗，或填充油箱REFILL/开启钻头DRILL。右侧面板可以挖矿，挖矿有几率出白方块等各种奖励。开启钻头后会增加深度DEPTH，随着深度增加挖矿出奖励的几率会不断提高 FACTORY：制造厂，在SHOP中购买材料，在RECIPES中点击道具右侧的SHOW RECIPE，根据合成表进行道具合成。在PRODUCERS菜单中可以放置PRODUCERS分类的道具，放置后每秒自动产出各类资源 HEADQUARTERS：总部，在MILITARY可以提升技能最高等级。在TECHNOLOGY中购买主板升级主板硬件后，可以在SOFTWARE中研究新功能 LABORATORY：实验室，研究各种元素可以解锁一些新的技能或元素加成，每个元素玩法都不太一样 WORKSHOP：工坊，可以装备技能，左侧BLUEPRINT列表中是已装备的技能，右侧是已获得未装备的技能。每个技能可以消耗蓝方块进行升级 CONSTRUCTION FIRM：建筑公司，建造或升级各类建筑物 其他功能目前还没解锁，感觉工坊和矿井比较重要。工坊可以提升技能的初始等级，矿井可以提供大量资源。

120小时了，我觉得如果英语不错的话其实还是值得一玩的，不过很多游戏乐趣在前十几甚至几十小时都体会不到 对于新手而言，如果英语能力过关建议先耐下性子仔细阅读power plant，laboratory和factory是如何运行的，然后如果有不清楚的地方及时查Wiki或者上discord问 以下是原评价：单就idle类游戏而言，Clicker Heroes已然达到了一个巅峰，以至于很难再有游戏能以相对更简单的机制带来更高的游戏性 经过了近50小时的挂机，我说一下新的感受 首先是太肝了，资源的主要来源是推图和游戏内放置，消耗时间太多，不过可以去玩别的游戏把它放在这里 其次是有关电厂，工厂和实验室这三个玩法的一点抱怨。三个玩法要产出可观的收益需要为数巨大的资源消耗，然后还要阅读超长的文本来搞清楚这些玩法究竟是如何运作并为你的岛屿带来收益的。相比于总体结构还算清晰的电厂而言，工厂高达10层的复杂合成树与实验室中不明所以的空气实验和消耗巨大的exotic实验对一个休闲向的游戏来说简直是灾难。 综上，目前以60小时的体验来说我仍然不是很推荐这一游戏，因为它在同样的学习成本与时间消耗的条件下带来的娱乐远低于其他的idle类游戏 有英语阅读能力和耐心的建议去Wiki看一眼，打死我都想不到作者塞了这么多东西 纠正一下，实验室的12个实验中，只有universal实验需要一点规划能力，darkness，gem和exotic实验需要耐心，其他实验砸资源就完事了

之前就玩过这种类似的塔防游戏，特别是那种自动化的，我这种懒人特别喜欢，也不用造那种传送带运资源，特别爽。但是没有中文就很难受。 WORKSHOP（工坊）：在里面可以装备技能和升级技能，但是最多只能升到100，有HEADQUARTERS（总部）后就可以在里面升级阶段,之后你就可以升级到200级，但是所有方块会请零，所以在升级前要在FACTORY（工厂）做多点蓝色方块电路板，以防不够资源升级。右侧是你现有的技能，左侧是BLUEPRINT（列表），里面是你已装备的技能，刚开始最多只能装六个技能，但是在升级WORKSHOP（工坊）后就可以装更多技能。 FACTORY（工厂）：你可以用红色方块购买材料，并用这些材料合成机器或电路板。制造出电路板后放在右侧第三个选项Producers就可以收集方块了。第五个选项Refining可以用工人来获取任意等级的Ore（就是那些各种颜色的像鸡块的东西），但是要使用颜色才能制造Ore，例如你想要制造Ore【T4】（那个蓝色的），你就得要四种不同的颜色才能制造，后面的以此类推，Ore【T7】就要七种不同的颜色，Ore【T9】就要九种不同的颜色。颜色可以在MINE（矿场）中通过挖矿获得。升级FACTORY（工厂）后就可以在左侧解锁更多的空间制造东西，下方也可以存储更多的材料，商店也会更新，合成配方也会增多。 MINE（矿场）：你可以用橙色方块来升级属性，分别是一秒能挖多深，能存多少油和一秒消耗多少油。点击DRILL就可以开始挖矿了，右侧分别是显示你得到这些东西的几率，x个橙色方块能解开一个格子，一秒能拿多少这种颜色和x个颜色能换一个方块。这里的x可以通过揭开格子减少，例如你要十个橙色方块才能揭开一个格子，当你拿到减少揭开格子所需要的橙色方块时，你就只需要九个橙色方块就能揭开一个格子了（最低为一个）。颜色同理，只要拿到那个道具，就可以变成1999个颜色换一个方块了（最低为一个）。上方是其它颜色的选择，但是你必须先建造了那个建筑物才能获取那个颜色。不过最好不要换太多方块，否则就没有颜色来制造Ore了。有非常小的机率获得Exotic Skills（那个紫粉相间的方块）。升级MINE（矿场）后除了钻头挖矿的速度增加就没什么用了（大概）。 LABORATORY（实验室）：可以通过研究各种元素得到一些新的技能或元素加成，每个元素玩法都不太一样，升级LABORATORY（实验室）后可以研究的元素增加。 HEADQUARTERS（总部）：在MILITARY可以升级阶段并提升技能最高等级，但是会清除所有方块（不包括电路板，工人，材料，Exotic Skills（那个紫粉相间的方块）等级和技能点）。在TECHNOLOGY中购买主板升级主板硬件后，可以在SOFTWARE中研究新功能，升级HEADQUARTERS（总部）可以增加主板硬件。 POWER PLANT（发电站）：在POWERGRID中建造设施产生电力，在NETWORK中消耗电力提升其他建筑物效率，升级POWER PLANT（发电站）后可以用更多的设备发电和储备电量。 CONSTRUCTION FIRM（建筑公司）：建造或升级各类建筑物。当HEADQUARTERS（总部）中的MILITARY达到第三阶段时可以把CONSTRUCTION FIRM（建筑公司）升至四级，然后就可以建造SHIPYARFD（码头）和STATUE OF CUBOS（Boss战）。 TRADING POST（交易所）：可以用任意方块换任意方块，交易后可以获得箱子，箱子可以配合浅蓝色方块在TRADING REWARDS中升级属性。升级后看不出来有多大的改变。 STATUE OF CUBOS（Boss战）：可以挑战BOSS，可以用黑色方块来升级自身属性，不和WORKSHOP（工坊）里所有的技能相通，只能使用里面自带的属性。升级STATUE OF CUBOS（Boss战）后可升级的属性增多。打败BOSS后可以获得Exotic Skills（那个紫粉相间的方块），然后解锁二阶段BOSS。注意！不能重复打一个阶段来刷Exotic Skills（那个紫粉相间的方块）。 SHIPYARFD（码头）：可以通过升级知道利润率（大概），然后可以选择运什么货过来，比如白色方块，Exotic Skills（那个紫粉相间的方块）Gems（那个蓝和浅蓝色相间的方块），每个时间都有特定的货，比如五分钟只能得到白色方块，一天能得到Exotic Skills（那个紫粉相间的方块）和Gems（那个蓝和浅蓝色相间的方块）。不过，利润率很低时所有的货都会降低数量，例如你本来能得到5000个白色方块，利润率降低后五分钟就只能运到3000个了，不过过久了利润率也会随着时间增加。升级SHIPYARFD（码头）后也没有多大变化。 MUSEUM（博物馆）：你可以购买宝石来增加攻击各种方块的增益，三个同样的宝石可以合成更高级的，三个更高级的可以合成更加高级的......升级MUSEUM（博物馆）后可以增加放宝石的栏位。 ARCADE（游戏中心）：可以通过玩游戏赚取游戏币，配合粉色方块可以购买技能，升级ARCADE（游戏中心）后可以解锁新的游戏。 主界面左边第五个是工人（只有白色方块不带眼镜的那个）如果没有就是没有升级阶段，里面可以用Gems（那个蓝和浅蓝色相间的方块）来增加工人，刚开始只能两个工人，但是升级阶段后就可以变为三个，右下角是升级工作速度，点击·工人方块左边那个一直在转的圈圈可以更换工作速度（前提是你有升级工作速度）。点击Task下面的白色框框就可以制定工作内容，可以多个工人进行单个或多个工人进行多个任务。 主界面左边第四个是装饰，可以通过解锁地图来解锁更多装饰，一个装饰可以增加百分之一白色方块的产出。 以上就是我目前知道的所有关于The Perfect Tower II这款游戏的内容，如果有错误可以提出，将来如果发现了新的内容也会追加留言。

The "Tower Defense" tag on this game is a nearly COMPLETE misnomer. There IS a "tower" and it does "defend", but the player has next to zero involvement with that portion of the game. You just set up perks for the tower and then let it run for infinity. What this game ACTUALLY is, is an idler/clicker game. Either just watching the tower run indefinitely or trying to set up a bunch of nonsensical currency generation at your base. Very boring, very grindy, very illogical, very uninvolved. OH! Aaaaand it even has a ridiculous prestige system! Y'know, so you can do all that boring, uninvolved grind AAAALLLLL over again. And again..... And again. FREE is a good price here. Still feels like a complete waste of time and effort though.

Trash. I discovered this game from DangerouslyFunny's youtube channel, and I can't, in a good faith, recommend playing this game. It's purely a dopamine trap and nothing more. It has a very strong start since the first thing it does is it introduces you to the tower defense minigame, which is something you're here likely for. It has a fairly unique module system, which allows you to diversify your tower and create unique strategies for the various tower defense levels. Moreover, you can upgrade your modules outside of the tower defense game in the workshop building to get a headstart in future games. Perhaps now you're wondering where does it all go wrong? Well, the opinions on the subject may vary, but for me, the downfall starts with the tiering system in the headquarters building, as it's a foreshadowing to the theme of this game. Whenever you want to tier up, you have to pay the ultimate sacrifice of giving up all of your resources and having your modules reset to the minimum level. Upgrading your modules takes time, so this is a major setback, especially since you need strong modules to get resources early on. The bandaid for this issue is that you can get a military perk which prevents the module reset below a certain point, but this doesn't fix it entirely since you will still end up wasting a lot of time building the modules back up. Sadly, this is just the beginning of the endless struggle, the devs have an unhealthy obsession with the prestige system in games, so they are shoehorned in a few areas in this game. I'm surprised that there isn't an option to prestige your entire game in exchange for some powerful boosts, given this big obsession with prestiges. This game suffers from having a very poor progression system. You start the game with just the basic tower defense minigame, but as you begin to develop your little island, you will be flooded with new buildings extremely quickly, many of which have absolutely nothing to do with the tower defense game itself, it's an unnecessary feature bloat that just overwhelms new players and makes them lose the desire to keep playing the game, and then once you unlock Military Tier 5, further progression slows down to a crawl and the gameplay becomes far less satisfying every time from that point on. Rather than having a simple and natural linear progression, this game has some kind of strange logarithmic progression. The buildings tend to be very confusing, and the ingame tutorial is extremely unhelpful since it's just an information dump that you will most likely skip through, you're off better getting your info from the wiki or from random youtube videos. Factory and Power Plant are easily the biggest offenders to the feature bloat, why do I have to waste time building power grids or craft a billion different things with such a horrible UI in a supposedly tower defense game?! Statue of Cubos and Laboratory are a hit and miss for me, some experiments in the lab are fun but some are extremely confusing and unintuitive, the boss fights in the Statue are extremely tedious, they could be fun otherwise, but they are also very distracting for the genre of the game since they play nothing like a tower defense game and more like a low effort flash game on newgrounds. Arcade is a horrible building, it should be removed and replaced. Mine, Trading Post and Shipyard seem to be the only buildings that don't seem intrusive to the actual gameplay, but for Mine you might want to assign workers to automate the progress. Workshop is fine, but my main issue with it is that it has no presets for the tower. I hate having to swap around 50 or so different modules everytime just so I can do a challenge, I can't understand why has this not been streamlined anyhow. Headquarters are a bit hit and miss for me when it comes to contracts. Contracts give the player a multiplier to resources earned, provided they fulfill certain requirements with their module set. On one hand, this is a great way to reward the player for being able to dominate a level with restrictions, on the other hand it just kills player creativity, since playing with a fun set can possibly disqualify you from being eligible for a contract which multiplies your resource yield. In case you're wondering, you can even have multiple contracts active at once, which leads to a massive increase in resource farming compared to not having any, so missing out on them is a big deal. I also hate the military tiers due to the aforementioned prestige nonsense and due to very dubious prestige requirements (MT6 requires you to kill a boss in the statue of Cubos, which for many would be a deal breaker). Personally, I really tried to enjoy this game, but I just couldn't do it. Most of the time I was just farming tower testing with the game minimized and while doing something else to pass the time just to push me a little bit further. After hitting MT6, progress has felt just so incredibly slow that it has soured whatever desire I might have had to continue the game. I've heard that the game gets better after MT7 or MT8 or so, but my argument to that is that I shouldn't have to wait such a long time to finally start enjoying myself, a game should be fun at all levels, and this game lacks that. The only real positive here is that this game is entirely free, and the ingame microtransactions are either for pure cosmetics, or for global boosts that affect everyone, so there is no P2W. I might reconsider my stance in the future if the developers make the progression more natural and remove the bad features, but my hopes aren't high, especially since they seem to consider the tower defense part of the game as a minor feature when it's the whole reason I've even played this to begin with. If you want a good tower defense game, you're still off better playing Bloons TD6 even if it has a worse monetization system and requires a purchase to play to begin with, at least they don't force you to build insane power grids to power up an entire island or craft items with extremely convoluted and complicated recipes that require a PhD to understand

The tower knows where it is at all times. It knows this because it knows where it isn't. By subtracting where it is from where it isn't, or where it isn't from where it is (whichever is greater), it obtains a difference, or deviation. The guidance subsystem uses deviations to generate corrective commands to drive the tower from a position where it is to a position where it isn't, and arriving at a position where it wasn't, it now is. Consequently, the position where it is, is now the position that it wasn't, and it follows that the position that it was, is now the position that it isn't. In the event that the position that it is in is not the position that it wasn't, the system has acquired a variation, the variation being the difference between where the tower is, and where it wasn't. If variation is considered to be a significant factor, it too may be corrected by the GEA. However, the tower must also know where it was. The tower guidance computer scenario works as follows. Because a variation has modified some of the information the tower has obtained, it is not sure just where it is. However, it is sure where it isn't, within reason, and it knows where it was. It now subtracts where it should be from where it wasn't, or vice-versa, and by differentiating this from the algebraic sum of where it shouldn't be, and where it was, it is able to obtain the deviation and its variation, which is called error.

作为IDLE类游戏是过于另类的。 游戏的主线毫无疑问还是TowerTesting，乍看是通过各种方式提升攻防、元素加成，获取更多的模组构建塔的build，达到更高层的测试等级。 但实际体验下来没有构建build的过程，一方面模组之间没什么传统意义上的联动，导致测试本身只是纯数值的校验，这从本质上就已经摧毁了塔防的核心玩法，一切只是为了数值，为了那一列元素攻防服务。塔防只是一个形式上的变化。 接着是软件部分对波次速度的加成，导致从中期开始游戏的玩法和前期产生了非常大的变化，可以说我就是从这里失去了自己对模组进行build的能力的，我看不懂我要怎么build才是有意义的。 再者Workshop的操作也很繁琐，逼你不得不去用别人的蓝图来过关。总之我认为作者就没有想让玩家去自己研究、凑build的想法。 不过这也无关紧要，毕竟大部分IDLE游戏的表面核心机制五花八门，但本质都是数值增量的校验，所以也无妨，但我认为塔防这个词条是很不贴切的。 最主要的问题是游戏内包含了太多无聊的，一定需要人为介入的部分。包括：部分实验（光暗通用宝石等），BOSS（最烂的部分，无聊透顶）。 我并非认为IDLE类游戏中所有人为介入的地方都是没意义的，相反，上手操作才是从IDLE中获取乐趣的核心，也就是“低效的操作—>低效的挂机—>高效的操作—>高效的挂机”这样的不断循环。 但这样的设计需要考虑，玩家操作的地方不能太无聊，相比之下，工厂部分的合成还算是里面最有意思的地方了，它不是一个独立的解密小游戏，而是和所有的系统结合起来，挖矿给你原矿，精炼、合成到高级矿。然后制作高级设备提高精炼效率、机器效率。最后获得更多的方块产出。 再者本身合成、制造这种游玩方式也是比较有意思的。 反过来看看，实验室部分的所有实验都是独立的，完成每个实验中的指标后、给你相似的加成，这很有趣吗我很难不想问作者。再看看boss，打的我快睡着了。最后我不得不压榨所有的工人没日没夜的在矿井里挖矿，提供我更多的奇异宝石就是为了不去打那个烂到爆的boss。 最后的问题就是主次不分。IDLE类游戏中如何把非自动的东西进行自动化，是很关键的转折，游戏内提供了工人来帮你进行，既然如此，AI脚本是想让我去做什么？你完全可以把所有的非自动化的部分抽象为工人能够完成的任务，然后把工人作为自动化的核心。 或者你就好好去做AI脚本的部分，提供一个可读性更强的，而不是现在这样甚至需要去精确到像素、点击的脚本系统，这样的东西没有人愿意去研究去写的。 综上，这个游戏真的可以说是我玩过最恶心的IDLE游戏，恶心在它让我经历了很不错的前几十小时的体验，然后用中后期的烂透了的系统来折磨我，让我不得不放弃存档。 最后补充一个浓缩度很高的攻略：https://github.com/ExpertLove/perfect-tower2-full-guide

That single issue alone soured the entire experience. The community is no rescue regardless. Ask a question in chat and you'll be pointed to Discord's pinned topics, a sprawling, disorganized archive you have to excavate just to find a partial answer that may still not make sense without context you don't have yet. It's a game that punishes curiosity rather than rewarding it. Your time is better spent elsewhere.

Developed and published by Fire Sword Studios, The Perfect Tower II takes the modest premise of defending a single structure and expands it into one of the most feature-rich incremental experiences available on Steam. At first glance, it appears to be a simple tower defense title with idle elements, but it gradually reveals itself as an intricate blend of city building, automation, resource management, and strategic progression. The game constantly rewards curiosity, encouraging players to experiment with its many systems rather than simply chasing higher numbers. What makes it particularly compelling is how naturally each mechanic unlocks and feeds into another, creating a gameplay loop that remains engaging long after the opening hours. The progression system is arguably the game's greatest accomplishment. Players begin with limited capabilities, but over time they establish an entire settlement around their tower, unlocking specialized facilities that provide research opportunities, resource production, and advanced customization options. The island headquarters steadily transforms into a thriving operation, and every new building introduces meaningful mechanics instead of acting as a superficial upgrade station. The sense of advancement is substantial, giving players the satisfaction of watching both their tower and their supporting infrastructure evolve into highly efficient machines. Unlike many idle games that eventually rely on repetitive resets, The Perfect Tower II continuously introduces new objectives that maintain momentum throughout its lengthy campaign. Combat remains an essential component of the experience, with players defending their tower against waves of increasingly dangerous enemies across numerous environments. The game offers multiple gameplay modes, including endless challenges and sandbox-style experimentation, ensuring there is always something to pursue regardless of preferred playstyle. Tower customization is extensive, allowing players to develop specialized builds that prioritize damage output, survivability, or utility. Boss encounters add additional variety and serve as major progression milestones. While the combat itself is relatively straightforward compared to dedicated tower defense games, it functions effectively as the foundation upon which the rest of the game's systems are built. A standout feature is the game's emphasis on automation. Rather than manually managing every aspect of progression indefinitely, players can gradually create automated workflows that handle tasks independently. This transforms the experience from a traditional idle game into something closer to a management simulator. There is immense satisfaction in reaching the point where carefully planned systems begin operating without intervention, allowing players to focus on larger strategic decisions. The automation tools possess a surprising level of depth and may initially feel daunting, but they ultimately become one of the most rewarding aspects of the entire package. Players who enjoy optimization and efficiency will likely spend dozens of hours refining their setups. The Perfect Tower II also benefits from its commitment to variety. Beyond tower defense and automation, the game incorporates numerous side activities and progression paths that prevent the experience from becoming monotonous. Exploration, mini-games, research projects, and hidden mechanics are scattered throughout the island, creating a sense of discovery that is uncommon within the genre. Fire Sword Studios has clearly designed the game with long-term engagement in mind, and that philosophy is evident in nearly every aspect of its design. Its ongoing support and community-focused development have further strengthened the title over time, resulting in a game that feels alive and continually improving. However, the game's ambition occasionally works against it. The overwhelming number of systems can become difficult to manage, especially for newcomers unfamiliar with incremental or automation-heavy titles. Menus are packed with information, and the user interface sometimes struggles to communicate priorities effectively. There are moments when progression feels slower than necessary, particularly during transitions between major milestones. Some players may also find themselves spending more time navigating menus than actively engaging with the tower defense component. These shortcomings do not significantly detract from the overall experience, but they can make the learning curve steeper than expected. From a presentation standpoint, The Perfect Tower II adopts a clean and functional visual style that prioritizes readability over spectacle. Its graphics are simple yet effective, ensuring that important information remains accessible even when numerous systems are operating simultaneously. The soundtrack complements the relaxed pacing with understated background music that suits lengthy play sessions. While it may not impress players looking for cutting-edge visuals, the game's aesthetic fits its design philosophy perfectly. Ultimately, The Perfect Tower II succeeds because of its willingness to embrace complexity while still maintaining a satisfying core gameplay loop. It is a title that respects the player's time and intelligence, offering countless hours of experimentation, optimization, and discovery. Fire Sword Studios has delivered a remarkably ambitious project that stands out within both the idle and tower defense genres. Although its extensive systems and occasionally cumbersome interface may not appeal to everyone, players who appreciate deep progression mechanics will find an experience that continues to reward investment long into the late game. Rating: 8/10
